before.text: | `web/scripts/assert-no-auth-token.mjs`     | Fails the build when `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`'s value is in a file under `.next/static`, which browsers download (section 4).                                            |

- **The token never reaches a browser file.** `web/scripts/assert-no-auth-token.mjs` runs at the end
  of `web`'s `build` script, after the design-system CSS check, and fails the build when the token's
  value appears in any file under `.next/static`, which browsers download. It prints the files,
  never the value. Without the token (CI, previews, local builds) it has nothing to check, so only
  the production build on Vercel runs it for real. The token is safe today without it — Next.js
  copies only `NEXT_PUBLIC_…` variables into the page, the token is read only in `next.config.ts`,
  and the wrapper adds only its own `_sentry*` values to the bundle — but nothing else would fail if
  a later change put it there.

- **The token check:** `tooling/assert-no-auth-token.test.mjs`, a sibling of
  `tooling/assert-design-system-css.test.mjs` under `pnpm run test:tooling`. With a fake token, a
  fake `.next/static` file that holds it fails the check, and the output names the file but never
  the value; clean files pass, and so does a build with no token.

- How Sentry 11 removes a tag: that `Sentry.setTag('instruments', undefined)` leaves no
  `instruments` key in the report that is sent.

items.scenario: You add a line to `web/app/play/page.tsx` that passes a server value to `PlayerShell` as a prop, and by mistake the value is `process.env.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`. The production build on Vercel stays green: the token check reads the 31 files under `.next/static` and finds nothing, because the token sits in `.next/server/app/play.html` and `play.rsc`. Every visitor to `/play` now downloads your Sentry token inside the page, and anyone who reads the page source can create releases and upload source maps in your Sentry organization.
items.corrections: None of the reviewers' claims is wrong. Two refinements: (1) the drafts walk all of `.next/server`, not only `.next/server/app`. The content is the same, because the 404 and 500 pages under `.next/server/pages` are byte copies of `server/app/_not-found.html` and `_global-error.html` (and after this spec, `_global-error.html` renders our own `global-error.tsx`); the wider folder also names the copies browsers receive, and the server-only bundles beside them cost nothing to read. (2) `.next/server/app` also holds server-only files (`page.js`, manifests, `.meta`); the files browsers download there are the `.html`, `.rsc` and `.segments/*.segment.rsc` files.
items.notes_for_triage: Two options. Option 1 (recommended by both reviewers, SEC-1 and ADV-3): the folders browsers download — `.next/static`, `.next/server`, `public/` — which is exactly ADD-5's 'any file a browser downloads'. Option 2 (the security-lens question): every file under `.next` except `.next/cache`, plus `public/` — one rule with no folder list, wider than ADD-5 (it also fails when the token sits in a server-only file such as required-server-files.json, for example if someone puts it in next.config's `env`). The evidence supports both. Nothing found would make option 2 fail a normal production build (Sentry 11.0.0 and 11.4.0 read the token in one place; the serialized config drops the hook's function), but that is read from source, not run, so option 2 adds a 'To verify' item. Flip to option 2 if the owner prefers no folder list to keep current (a hand-kept list must follow Next's layout: the reviewers' `server/app` already leaves out `server/pages`, where Next copies the 404 and 500 pages); keep option 1 if the check should match ADD-5's words exactly. Either way an encoded copy (base64, URL-encoded) still passes: a residual, not raised here. The plan note recorded for ADD-5 ('walks .next/static') changes with either option. Interaction with FYI-16 option 1: once `errorHandler` throws, a local build with a fake token fails at Sentry's release step before the token check runs, so option 2's 'To verify' build would run with the default handler. A Drop leaves the gap: a server component that renders the token into `/` or `/play` ships it with a green build, against ADD-5's decision.

items.scenario: The separate domain ticket points `notationhero.com` at the site, and visitors start using it. A visitor opens a file that is not a score and sees "Error E103", but Sentry discards the report because `notationhero.com` is not in Allowed Domains: no issue opens, no email arrives, and Release Health stops counting visits. The only trace is a "Disallowed Domain" count on Sentry's Stats page, which you have no reason to open, so the empty issue list reads as a healthy site.
items.corrections: Severity: P2, not P1 (ADV-1). Nothing ships broken: at ship time production has one host and step 3 lists it, so the Goal holds; reports stop only after the separate domain ticket ships, or for a deployment's own URL. Everything else holds: `*.notationhero.com` does match the bare domain (PRO-1, confirmed by running Relay's matcher), error reports and Release Health pings are both discarded, and only Stats shows it. One refinement to ADV-1's fix: the reminder must name the `www` host (or use the wildcard), because a bare `notationhero.com` entry does not match `www.notationhero.com`.
items.notes_for_triage: Two options. Option 1 (product-lens, PRO-1): list `notation-hero-web.vercel.app` and `*.notationhero.com` now, so the domain ticket has nothing to remember. Option 2 (adversarial, ADV-1): list only today's host and tell the domain ticket to add the new one; that works only if that ticket's implementer reads this spec, so README.md:156 or the Jira ticket would need the same reminder, a file §7 does not list. The evidence favours option 1: the matching is confirmed, only the owner controls DNS for notationhero.com, and the extra subdomains the wildcard admits (the ADR's planned `api.` and `auth.` hosts) run no page with this DSN. Flip to option 2 if the owner wants the list to name only hosts that serve the site today. The step-6 change is the same in both options. The reviewers' related question (should the domain ticket repeat step 6 from the new domain, so one E103 proves reports still arrive?) is cheap and fits either option, but belongs to that ticket. A Drop leaves the domain move as a silent end of monitoring, and step 6 fails with no visible cause if run from a deployment's own URL.

items.scenario: A future bug puts a track name, such as `Lead Guitar`, into an error message that the names filter misses, and you see it in an issue title and in its alert email. Nothing in the spec says how long Sentry keeps that report or how to remove it, so it stays readable in the project for 30 days. Sentry cannot delete that one report: you delete the whole issue with the trash icon on its page, delete the email, and fix the filter before the next deploy.
items.corrections: The suggested text says the report 'is deleted in Sentry at once, together with its alert email'. Sentry cannot delete one report, only the whole issue that holds it (with every other report in it), and the alert email is in the owner's mailbox, not in Sentry. The draft says both. The 30-day figure is right for the Developer plan.

before.text:
- **Source maps** (D4): `withSentryConfig` uploads them after `next build` (Turbopack builds are
  supported from `@sentry/nextjs` 10.13) and deletes them from the deploy by default
  (`sourcemaps.deleteSourcemapsAfterUpload: true`). "Hide source content" stays **off**: the
  repository is public, so hiding the code in Sentry protects nothing and removes the code around
  each error line.
- **Release Health pings on every visit**, not only on a crash. The home-page copy says so.

after_draft.text:
- **Source maps** (D4): `withSentryConfig` uploads them after `next build` (Turbopack builds are
  supported from `@sentry/nextjs` 10.13) and deletes them from the deploy by default
  (`sourcemaps.deleteSourcemapsAfterUpload: true`). "Hide source content" stays **off**: the
  repository is public, so hiding the code in Sentry protects nothing and removes the code around
  each error line.
- **A failed upload stops the deploy.** By default, Sentry's build plugin only logs a release or
  upload step that fails: the build goes on, and the maps are deleted anyway, so that release's
  own frames stay minified, and only a line in Vercel's build log says so. With `errorHandler` (in
  the snippet below), the production build fails at that step instead: Vercel keeps the previous
  deployment live, and a redeploy tries again. The cost: while Sentry is down or the token is
  revoked, no production deploy succeeds until Sentry answers again or the token is replaced.

after_draft.option: 2 (keep the default; record it as a known limit)
after_draft.text:
- **Release Health pings on every visit**, not only on a crash. The home-page copy says so.
- **A failed source-map upload is silent.** If the release or upload step fails during a
  production build (a revoked token, an outage at Sentry, a rate limit), Sentry's build plugin
  logs one line in Vercel's build log, the deploy goes ahead, and the maps are deleted anyway: that
  release's own frames stay minified. Setup step 6 proves the upload once, not on every deploy.

items.scenario: You revoke the Sentry token by mistake, then merge a pull request. Vercel's production build logs one line, "An error occurred. Couldn't finish all operations", deletes the `.map` files and deploys anyway. From then on every error from that release shows our own frames minified, `PlayerShell.tsx` never appears, and nothing told you. With the throwing `errorHandler`, the same deploy fails on Vercel instead, the previous deployment stays live, and the failed deploy tells you to fix the token.
items.corrections: None. One addition: under option 1, a failure to finalize the release or to record the deploy (both on by default on Vercel) also stops the build, not only the upload; the default set-commits step does not, because Sentry marks it as one that never throws.
items.notes_for_triage: Two options. Option 1 (recommended by the reviewer, ADV-4): `errorHandler` rethrows, so a failed release or upload step stops the production deploy. The cost: while Sentry is down or the token is revoked, no production deploy succeeds; removing SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN from Vercel lets one through without maps, since the hook is off without it. Option 2: keep Sentry's default and record it as a known limit. The evidence confirms the reviewer's facts; the choice is a trade-off between deploy availability and readable stack traces, and nothing in the evidence decides it. Interaction with F-32 option 2: its 'To verify' build with a fake token would fail at the release step under option 1, so that check runs with the default handler. Sentry's own doc comment says the default already throws; the plan should not rely on it. A Drop leaves a failed upload visible only as one line in Vercel's build log; setup step 6 proves the upload once.
